title: Heatwave reveals lost archaeological sites across Wales
description: RCAHMW said the east and north-east of Wales has been very dry since mid-May, while much of  west and south Wales stayed fairly damp and green.However
body: RCAHMW said the east and north-east of Wales has been very dry since mid-May, while much of  west and south Wales stayed fairly damp and green.However, the series of heatwaves in late June scorched off grasslands across Wales.It revealed "monuments ranging from prehistoric long barrows and forts to Roman buildings and even First World War practice trenches," they said.  The national archive for the Welsh historic environment has released photographs of Driver's discoveries following flights from Haverfordwest and Caernarfon airport in June and July. "This year has been pretty windy across Wales, so some of the longer trips to record cropmarks have made for challenging flying," Driver said.   "Sometimes the cropmarks are so clear they jump out as we orbit the aircraft around to photograph them. But some parts of Wales are now so dry that the cropmarks can be faint and pretty hard to see."He added: "In these cases we digitally rebalance the colour bands of the image,  really making the archaeology 'pop' and reveal previously hidden details – these images appear as black and white".

schema.headline: Heatwave reveals lost archaeological sites across Wales

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Gabriel Langton injury overshadows gymnastics silver
description: A sickening injury to England's Gabriel Langton overshadowed his team's silver medal in the men's team gymnastics final at the Commonwealth Games in G
body: A sickening injury to England's Gabriel Langton overshadowed his team's silver medal in the men's team gymnastics final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.The 19-year-old, from the City of Birmingham Gymnastics Club, needed lengthy treatment on the mat after a horrible fall in the final rotation of the evening at The Arena.Langton fell head first to the floor after missing his catch on the horizontal metal bar, three metres in the air, leading to a lengthy delay to the action as he was tended to by up to a dozen medical staff.He was eventually led away on a trolley after being moved on to a stretcher with his head and neck braced and left to huge applause from the packed crowd who had spent much of the previous 10 minutes in hushed silence.Langton was seen to be conscious and moving his legs and arms before leaving the arena floor, while team officials later said he was moving and speaking to doctors.In a statement, Team England said: "We are grateful to the medical teams who responded immediately to provide assistance."He has been taken to hospital and we will share more information when it is available."When competition resumed, his England team-mates were unable to overhaul their deficit to Canada who claimed their first gold medal in the event in 20 years, having finished second to England at the past two games.Langton, a late call-up to Team England in the place of the injured six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock,  was unable to join his teammates on the podium as England collected their silver medals.Team-mate Luke Whitehouse, who was first on to the apparatus after the competition restarted and posted a relatively low score of 11.700, said: "When something like that happens, you've just got to forget about it and reset. I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time." Whitehouse added: "From what we've heard, he's doing OK. Gymnastics is such a dangerous sport and things like this remind us of that. It's one of those things you have to put out of your mind."Felix Dolci, who helped Canada to gold and led qualifying for the all-around competition, said: "It's terrible but it goes to show that gymnastics is a very, very difficult and complicated sport. It's dangerous you know sometimes. "All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team. Pushing through this is definitely not easy, England stayed focussed, they stayed in the zone, a huge shout out to them because that's not an easy one. "For any gymnast that was on the field of play, seeing this not only is difficult, but something you never want to see. It goes to show how hard the sport is."Hamish Carter from Team Scotland - who narrowly missed out on a bronze medal to Australia in the final rotation - said: "I didn't actually see what happened. I'm just so happy that he's alright and, having experienced that, anything could have happened. "We've walked away with no medal but I'm thinking of Gabe in this moment."

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: Gabriel Langton injury overshadows gymnastics silver

title: Graduation outfits: Students tell us how to impress on a budget
description: "My mum is a designer so she made this for me," says Wendy. "It took her a week… I'm her daughter, so she had to put in every [effort]."Wendy says the
body: "My mum is a designer so she made this for me," says Wendy. "It took her a week… I'm her daughter, so she had to put in every [effort]."Wendy says the significance of graduation inspired her to create a custom look. "I feel like you have to because it's your day. We go through a lot to get a master's degree so you have to look your best on the day."Graduation also comes at a time when students are "the least financially resilient", says Allingham, as they have been absorbing the costs of studying all year.The maintenance loan falls short of living costs by an average of £502 per month, according to analysis by Save The Student, external. This gap is plugged - sometimes only partially - by parental support, part-time jobs and debt.Another factor that can increase the cost of graduation is buying an official photograph, with providers specified by your university, adds Allingham. "The price of photography on the day - it's extortionate."Professional packages at the University of Salford start at £30 - an image of the graduate is sent digitally - and the most expensive is £350. For that you receive about 20 prints with various mounts and frames of two images, one of the graduate and another with friends and family.Like Keerthana, Alicia Munhupedzi used the internet to find her dress - though it was a bit last minute."I thought, 'Where can I get a nice dress really quickly and cheaply?'" The answer? Depop, the second-hand clothing app popular among Gen Z shoppers that sold for $1.2bn (£890m) earlier this year.Like others, Alicia felt her outfit was important. "Graduation, it's a milestone thing, especially if you're not planning on doing a master's," she says. "So, to me, there was a pressure."So much so she couldn't sleep properly the night before her ceremony and woke at dawn to get ready. "I made it through today off two hours of sleep, water, good vibes, energy and a coffee."Knowing all eyes would be fixed on her when she was handed her degree, Keerthana says she was nervous for her graduation ceremony - but it passed more quickly than she thought it might."This is the only moment you get for yourself," she says. And was the 05:00 wake-up and two hours of getting ready worth it? "Yeah," Keerthana says, "I couldn't compromise on that."Additional reporting by Kate Berry and George Sandeman.

schema.headline: Graduation outfits: Students tell us how to impress on a budget

title: Five ways to make the most of the summer holidays with kids
description: Image source, Nilly DahliaImage caption, Nilly Dahlia says she wants her kids to enjoy a "nostalgic summer"ByEmily HoltThe six-week summer holidays ha
body: Image source, Nilly DahliaImage caption, Nilly Dahlia says she wants her kids to enjoy a "nostalgic summer"ByEmily HoltThe six-week summer holidays have officially begun and, for many parents, finding exciting but affordable activities for children can be tough. For most families in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the break has only just started. In Scotland, children have enjoyed some time off already, but will return to school earlier than those elsewhere in the UK.Here are five tips to help children get the most out of the next few weeks of summer. 1. Not every holiday has to be abroad A family's first instinct when summer is approaching may be to look at booking a trip abroad, but rising costs and travel expenses mean a holiday isn't feasible for everyone. Mags Rivett, director at Family Holiday Charity, which supports families with UK trips, says there are many benefits to arranging time away with children that don't require expensive travel. She says the social aspect of a holiday can help children develop their communication skills. "Lots of kids have never really had the opportunity to meet people outside of their own community," Rivett says. "But if you go somewhere that's got social facilities, it's a really important opportunity."She says getting recommendations from friends and family is a good place to start. Rivett gives the example of Skegness, a coastal holiday destination in Lincolnshire, accessible by train or coach, which her charity has supported families to visit.A family-of-four's accommodation in a holiday park there this August starts at around £750 for a week, while an off-peak return train from Manchester would cost around £280 for four.By contrast, a last-minute trip to Majorca for a family-of-four at that time starts from around £2,000. Better deals can usually be found booking further in advance.2. Prioritise the moments, not the cost Samantha Thomas, creator of Budget Mum UK, says she focuses on the time she can give her children, rather than the money she could spend on a day out. Thomas suggests focusing on your budget first to understand what you can comfortably spend, and then build your activities around that, to help remove any "stress or guilt" during the holidays. "Children don't need a six-week programme of expensive activities," Thomas says. "Some of the memories that they'll treasure most will come from simple things, like baking together or a picnic in the park, or building a den in the living room."Ingredients to bake fairy cakes with buttercream icing usually cost between £10 and £15 - depending on what you already have in the cupboard.For a picnic - or picky bits - prices can vary. But it can easily be done on a budget of around £5. Image source, Samantha ThomasImage caption, Samantha Thomas says treasured family memories can be created on a budgetTasneem Abdur-Rashid, an author and single mum of two, echoes Thomas' opinion and wants to relieve the pressure she puts on herself to do something different with her children every day. She says it's important to take time out, put work away, and spend one-on-one time with your children. This could be going to play in the park, or going swimming.Trips to local pools or lidos can cost around £6 for adults, and £3.50 for children.Abdur-Rashid says every night during the holidays she will play board games with her children, which blends quality time and fun. These can be picked up at local charity shops for very reasonable prices."You don't even have to leave the house for that," she says, "and they love it."3. Use what's available in your area Nilly Dahlia, a content creator and mum of three, says she prints out a six-week calendar with a range of activities for her kids during the holidays. As part of their "summer bucket list", they are planning to check out all the parks in the local area and she is prioritising low-cost activities throughout the summer. "I feel like there's this intense pressure to have Instagram-worthy holidays now," she says."What's wrong with just staying in the UK, staying out till sunset, riding your bike, just going to the river, like I did? I really want the kids to experience a nostalgic summer."Dahlia stresses there are many things on offer during the holidays that won't break the bank, such as free kids' meals in cafes and discounts on local travel. And there are often offers at bowling venues and cinemas, she says, while her family enjoys a movie night at home every Friday."They each have a bowl of popcorn and treats and we move the sofas into two rows so it's like a cinema."James Gray, communications and advocacy manager at Libraries Connected, says the summer holidays are also where libraries "come alive". He says libraries across the UK will hold the Summer Reading Challenge, encouraging kids to read more in a fun format, and many will be hosting events such as arts and crafts, performances and creative workshops, all for free. 4. Balance rest with some learningDahlia says she picks up books for her children to get them ready for the next school year. Her youngest will receive some chapter books to help them transition into Year 3, while her eldest is moving to secondary school, and Dahlia has prepped suitable books to bridge that gap from primary.She preps "summer baskets" which include puzzle books, reading books and snacks  to curb any boredom. "It's so important because by reading, they're still engaging their brain so they can go back to school in September, already having vocabulary in them."As a busy parent, Abdur-Rashid says she doesn't always have the time to do everything she'd like with her children, but structures their days to make sure they are always doing an activity. She allocates an hour a day for gaming which her boys enjoy, and then fills the rest of the time with playing, reading or writing. She also wants to foster a passion for reading in her kids, and allows them to not finish books they don't enjoy so reading doesn't become a "punishment".Image source, Tasneem Abdur-RashidImage caption, Author Tasneem Abdur-Rashid suggests parks and picnics for low-cost quality time with your childrenGavin Morgan, an education psychologist at University College London, says it's important to let children be "bored" during the holidays. "It's really important that they have opportunities to switch off from school and from that structure in order to experience and explore new things and get bored, because for some kids, that can really spark that creativity."For those entering exam years, Morgan says parents should have a conversation with their child about what they need to do and what suits them best. "The worst thing for parents to do is put their child under any kind of pressure, because they'll end up being switched off from learning," he says.He says parents should encourage their children to take a break from their education, so they return to school in September "feeling really confident and refreshed".5. Get ahead for the next holidays Thomas says she starts planning her summer budget well in advance. She does this by contributing a little bit of money every month into a "sinking fund" - a pot of money set aside for a specific purpose.This summer her budget is £500, and she sits down with her children to discuss how much they have budgeted and to brainstorm activities they can do together. "You've got that open dialogue, so they understand there's only a finite amount of money, and we've got a plan on how to do that best," she says.Thomas also uses cashback websites to get money back on things she has bought, which she says is "brilliant for hotels or travel". If you are planning a holiday, whether abroad or in the UK, Thomas stresses to plan and book in advance to get better deals. She also recommends looking at attractions within your local area before travelling further afield. Additional reporting by Hayley Clarke

schema.headline: Five ways to make the most of the summer holidays with kids

title: Tyson Fury vs Mariusz Wach: Briton wins low-key warm-up to keep Anthony Joshua fight on track
description: British heavyweight Tyson Fury stopped Mariusz Wach in a low-key bout in Thailand to keep a potential blockbuster fight with Anthony Joshua on track.
body: British heavyweight Tyson Fury stopped Mariusz Wach in a low-key bout in Thailand to keep a potential blockbuster fight with Anthony Joshua on track. The 37-year-old dominated for seven rounds at the Max Muay Thai Stadium in Pattaya - in front of no more than 1,500 fans - before the overmatched Wach, 46, retired on his stool at the start of the eighth. The 36th victory of his career moves Fury closer to a meeting with fellow Briton Joshua, who has his own comeback fight against Albanian Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia on Saturday."I went through my test tonight. Let's see if he can get through his," Fury said. Many expected 'the Gypsy King' to fly straight to Jeddah for Joshua's bout, with the pair potentially announcing their long-awaited showdown in the ring afterwards if Joshua wins.Instead, Fury said he was going home."I've got to face off with my wife. I've got to iron when I get home. I've been away for six out of the last seven months", he said. "I'm not going to Jeddah, I'm going home to my wife and kids. I'm going to regroup and hopefully we'll have a big fight signed next week."Questions still linger over where the all-British bout would take place, with Eddie Hearn saying Joshua's contract stipulates the UK, but industry whispers suggesting a venue in America."We'll head wherever we're going to head," Fury said."Who knows? It could be in Vegas, New York, Ireland, London. Who knows where the fight's going to be?"Fury's win over Wach was not broadcast live on any television or radio platform, and will instead form part of the third series of the Netflix reality show 'At Home With The Furys'.Fury has become a mainstream celebrity beyond boxing, with his outspoken personality, reality TV appearances and larger-than-life public image.But in Pattaya there was no pay-per-view build-up or millions watching from home.Earlier in the evening, the venue staged its regular programme of Muay Thai bouts before staff stripped away the canvas and transformed the ring for Fury's boxing card."We've all heard of the 'Thriller in Manila', you've heard of the 'Rumble in the Jungle' and you've heard of the punch-up in Pattaya," Fury said.There was something almost nostalgic about it all. A generation ago, boxing fans might have waited until the following morning to read the result in the newspapers.This time, reporters were refreshing social media, while the handful of journalists and YouTube channels inside the venue became the eyes and ears for everyone else.According to those updates, Fury controlled the opening rounds, although one clip posted on X showed Poland's Wach catching him with a right hand in the second.Another revealed pockets of empty seats - a striking contrast for a fighter who has packed Wembley Stadium with 96,000 fans and drawn 64,500 to Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.Another clip showed Fury, who said ticket profits would be donated to a local charity supporting disadvantaged children and students with disabilities, dictating the pace and repeatedly landing uppercuts at close range in the fifth.One reporter even claimed Fury paused to kiss Wach midway through the sixth round.It was not long before Wach and his corner had seen enough. Unable to withstand another three rounds of punishment, Wach was withdrawn to hand Fury his first stoppage victory since beating Derek Chisora in 2022.

schema.headline: Tyson Fury vs Mariusz Wach: Briton wins low-key warm-up to keep Anthony Joshua fight on track

title: The human cost of South Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveries
description: 'It eats away at my body': The human cost of S Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveriesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, South Korea's hug
body: 'It eats away at my body': The human cost of S Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveriesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, South Korea's huge delivery industry, powered by thousands of warehouse workers and riders, is under scrutinyByJake Kwon, Leehyun Choi and Hosu LeeReporting fromSeoulA week before her son died Park Mi-suk asked him to quit his job.For more than a year, the 27-year-old had been working overnight shifts at a warehouse for the country's largest online retailer, Coupang. He steered pallet movers with stacks of plastic bins and cardboard boxes across the sprawling space.In that time, Park says, her son lost 15kg and often complained of how tired he was.But Jang Deok-jun refused to quit. He compared his job to being on a seesaw: if he stepped down, his co-workers would struggle to keep going.The following week, Park found him unconscious and hunched over in the bath. "We pulled him out and performed first aid. We rushed him to hospital, where they declared him dead."Jang died of a heart attack. The state-run insurer that covers healthcare for workers, Comwel, blamed his death on overwork following an investigation.Park wishes she had noticed Jang's exhaustion sooner. "I didn't pay attention to my son's words, so I lost my son. But I hope others won't repeat the same mistake."Jang died in 2020 but six years on, Park is still fighting to end what she believes is the reason for his death: night-time deliveries.Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Jang Deok-jun was 27 years old when he died of a heart attackJang died as deliveries surged during the pandemic, which was often cited to explain his workload. But the working conditions for warehouse and delivery workers have been the subject of a growing national debate, with their union claiming that suspected deaths from overwork have continued.Night-time deliveries have become ubiquitous in hyper-connected South Korea, where shoppers are guaranteed delivery by 07:00 for orders placed before midnight. This convenience is thanks to a huge overnight workforce, from warehouse workers like Jang to delivery drivers.Several companies compete to offer speedy, cheap deliveries but the biggest is Coupang. Founded by a Korean-American, it became synonymous with online shopping in South Korea after 2015, when it started offering fresh produce overnight. It has grown to have an unrivalled network of warehouses and delivery trucks, with nearly 100,000 employees across the business.But increasingly, this industry is under scrutiny.Image source, BBC/Hosu LeeImage caption, Jang's mother Park Mi-suk says workers like her son are becoming invisibleBetween 2020 and May 2026, Comwel ruled that 46 warehouse and delivery workers, including Jang, died of a stroke or heart disease that count as work-related deaths. Jang aside, it's unclear how many of them worked overnight shifts.Comwel did not say how many of these cases were also investigated for the role of overwork, which only happens if the family asks for it in their claim. And not every case is referred to Comwel in the first place, so the data can be patchy.Previously Comwel data suggested that day-time delivery workers died of overwork and accidents at a higher rate than those who work overnight. But that is now questioned by those who say night-time deliveries are expanding fast, and there is not enough data to fully document their impact yet. The workers' union also argues that the latter is more harmful to health in the long-term.Night-time work is a probable cause of cancer globally, according to the UN's cancer research body, external. "Not only that, evidence has been accumulating that it also raises the risk of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and mental illness," says Kang Mo-yeol, professor of occupational medicine at the Catholic University of Korea.South Korea doesn't limit overnight working hours, unlike in the UK, where night-time delivery drivers cannot work more than 10 out of 24 hours. The Korean delivery workers' union called for a ban on overnight deliveries in 2025, but the union for Coupang's drivers says nearly all of their members prefer working at night. Some have children, elderly or ill family members to care for during the day and, more importantly, it pays better.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Coupang is the biggest of South Korea's online retailers "I can't do this for life because it eats away at my body," says Kim, a Coupang driver on a sub-contract, who did not want to share his real name. But he adds that his monthly salary of around 7m won ($4,600; £3,430) - nearly double the national average - makes it worth it.When the BBC met him at 22:00, he had already loaded his truck for the first round of deliveries.Driving through the narrow streets of Incheon city, west of the capital Seoul, he explains that he works from 21:00 to 07:00, five to six days a week.His schedule does not allow for a break. Every time the truck stops, he runs, package in hand. Nearly all drivers are paid by the number of packages they deliver and if they fail to make all deliveries by 07:00, they risk losing their "territory" to a competitor, he says.At first, his pregnant wife was scared he might fall asleep at the wheel. But he is used to it now, he insists, and he finds it easier to navigate the night's empty streets."We choose to deliver overnight for the money," Kim says. The way he sees it, those who are saying overnight deliveries should stop because they affect his health are ignoring the choice he has made. Image source, BBC/Hosu LeeImage caption, Kim said he is making good money as an overnight delivery driver, but his wife is worried he will fall asleep at the wheelBut men like Kim are becoming invisible, Jang's mother Park says, as the demand for fast deliveries grows, normalising the industry.Park spoke to the BBC outside Coupang's headquarters in Seoul's office district of Songpa. Standing alone in front of the gate, she told staff streaming out for lunch to remember her son and others like him. Few paid attention.Park says one of the challenges is how hard it is to hold employers accountable in cases like Jang's. She says it was on her to prove that her son had died from overwork, and Coupang was obligated to provide records, including security camera footage, to Comwel, but not her. After months of leaning on lawmakers and government agencies, she received Jang's work log and relevant CCTV footage.In the months before his death, Jang's working hours met the bar for how South Korean law defines deaths related to overwork: heart attacks or brain strokes after an average 60-hour-week over 12 weeks, or 64 hours a week in the four weeks leading up to death. Jang's overnight hours counted 30% more towards the calculation, according to Comwel's rules.Image source, BBC/Hosu LeeImage caption, Park outside Coupang's headquarters in Seoul, where she has been trying to draw attention to Jang's case As Park continued her fight, local media published what Coupang's former chief privacy officer claimed was a conversation with Chairman Bom Kim. In the leaked chat, Kim orders the executive to remove mentions of Jang "working hard" from internal reports: a phrase several employees used to describe Jang's final shift. Coupang called it a "groundless" claim by a disgruntled former executive.But the union accused the firm of covering up evidence and filed a criminal complaint. The police launched an investigation into Coupang in December 2025. Coupang denies the accusation, saying it had submitted everything that was requested and had fully cooperated with Comwel's investigation.By then, another high-profile case was in the headlines. Oh Seung-yong, 34, died after crashing his truck into a pole during a delivery run. It was an "occupational death", or work played a role, Comwel ruled.Oh's sister told parliament his work log showed that he had been working six days a week, more than 11 hours a day, and mostly at night. According to her, when their father had died days earlier, Oh delivered orders for another four hours before coming to hospital. He worked for a logistics company contracted by Coupang.Coupang says it restricts its employees to working for under 52 hours and gives sub-contracted drivers the full weekend off every two weeks. But the union alleges that this was not enforced by Oh's employer.The firm added that it fully pays for health check-ups for direct employees and sub-contracted drivers, and "has never had a single industrial accident death, which is the best safety record in the entire global logistics industry".Image source, SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Coupang boss Harold Rogers at South Korea's parliament Coupang CEO Harold Rogers was summoned to parliament in December 2025 over the deaths of Jang and Oh, as well as to answer for a recent data breach at his firm, involving 37.5 million users. The country's largest ever breach, it earned them a record $410m fine.During the televised hearing, Park demanded that Coupang's Chairman Kim be held accountable for her son's death, while Oh's sister asked for an apology from Rogers. He said he was "sorry" and offered his "deepest condolences". When Oh's sister pressed further, he was silent.The investigation into Coupang has also raised key questions for President Lee Jae Myung, who has a disability in his left arm from an old injury at a factory. He made it one of his priorities to reduce workplace injuries and deaths.Stories like Jang's and Oh's resonate deeply in South Korea, where gruelling work hours are no anomaly. It has one of the highest rates of workplace deaths among developed countries, a grim statistic it has been trying to improve for decades.The government has capped weekly work hours at 52 and passed a law to jail executives for negligence leading to workplace deaths. To break Coupang's stranglehold, the governing party even proposed relaxing existing restrictions so more retailers can deliver overnight. But the bill angered unions, activists and Park, who say the challenge goes beyond Coupang.Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Six years on from 27-year-old Jang's death, his mother still has his belongings"I've been haunting the streets since my son died," Park says.Because of all the time spent fighting for compensation and answers, she was forced to close her furniture-making business. She could no longer afford to live in her old home and moved to a rental apartment in Daegu city.She has kept all of Jang's belongings, including his collection of action figures. They sit in a box in her new apartment. She isn't ready to say goodbye yet, or to give up her fight.Recalling how Jang compared his work to riding a seesaw, where he held down one end, she says she sees it differently now. Jang and tens of thousands of workers like him are on one side for the convenience of the consumers on the other end, she says. "I hope we don't become a society where we close our eyes to others' sacrifice for a little convenience."

schema.headline: The human cost of South Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveries

title: Tour de France 2026: Tadej Pogacar wins on Alpe d'Huez
description: Defending champion Tadej Pogacar is on the verge of winning a record-equalling fifth Tour de France after taking a storming victory on stage 19 to Alp
body: Defending champion Tadej Pogacar is on the verge of winning a record-equalling fifth Tour de France after taking a storming victory on stage 19 to Alpe d'Huez.The UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider pulled more than three minutes back on a breakaway group on the hors category final climb up to the famous ski resort, which was flanked by thousands of spectators from all around the world. Pogacar, 27, is aiming to become the joint-most successful rider in the Tour's history with five wins, alongside Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain.Pogacar has a dominant lead over Belgium's Remco Evenepoel of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe of seven minutes 11 seconds, despite the Belgian's improved climbing form this year.Pogacar's Mexican team-mate Isaac del Toro remains third and in the white young riders' classification leader's jersey - nine minutes 42 seconds down.The peloton will take on Alpe d'Huez once again on Saturday for the three-week race's mountainous 'queen' stage, which includes an extra 2,000 metres of climbing."It was very cool to win up here - it was a crazy atmosphere all climb and I'm thankful for the team that I it could pull it off," said Pogacar."When I heard some of the guys [were] dropped when [team-mate] Felix [Grosschartner] set a super good pace at the beginning of the climb, I was already going full gas, as the breakaway was so strong. Every kilometre of Alpe d'Huez I had good legs and not many could follow [me]." Pogacar crossed the line six seconds ahead of France's Lenny Martinez of Bahrain-Victorious, who thumped his handlebars severnal times in frustration as he crossed the line.Ecuador's in-form rider Richard Carapaz of EF Education-Easypost, who won Thursday's stage to Ocieres Merlette, finished a further three seconds behind in third.A 40-plus strong breakaway had established a lead over the peloton and yellow-jersey wearer Pogacar by several minutes mid-stage, but the main pack began to slowly reel them in.It was Martinez, the USA's Sepp Kuss of Visma-Lease a Bike and a typically animated Carapaz who eventually emerged as the three seemingly set to battle for victory as they began Alpe d'Huez's legendary twisting ribbons of tarmac.But Pogacar had other ideas and set a record time on the final climb of 35 minutes 27 seconds - beating the time set by Italy's legendary Marco Pantani in 1997. Read more: Why are cycling's anti-doping tests being carried out at night?In setting his staggering time, Pogacar had taken off alone in pursuit of the remaining riders in the break, before finding rejuvenated British team-mate Adam Yates further up the climb to help pace him some of the way through the crowds, who were spilling dangerously on to the road within millimetres of the riders, who in turn were becoming ever more frustrated by the potential of a collision.Yates, 33, whose career includes a Tour stage win and time in the yellow jersey, showed great strength in leading the breakaway before becoming the perfect 'satellite' rider to help Pogacar on his late-stage charge. It comes just a few days after Yates fell ill and vomited after stage 16's time trial.He spent the subsequent two stages riding slowly at the very back of the field, losing nearly an hour in total overall.Typically riders would abandon the Tour in that kind of condition to avoid causing further illness, but Yates' tenacity did not go unnoticed."Adam gave me a good moral boost," said Pogacar. "I was so happy he is finally back after the day of the TT - he was so bad and I'm super happy to ride behind him on the climb."Yates, 33, has been a loyal domestique to Pogacar since 2023, and is contracted for another two seasons. His identical twin Simon retired in January after winning the 2025 Giro d'Italia three-week Grand Tour to add to his 2018 Vuelta a Espana victory.Further down the field Denmark's Mads Pedersen of Lidl-Trek remains it the green points jersey after stretching his lead over Belgium's Jasper Philipsen.Carapaz's combative riding sees him take over the polka-dot King of the Mountains jersey by one point from Pogacar.Tour de France stage 19 results 1. title: ICC top prosecutor removed over sexual misconduct allegations
description: Members of the International Criminal Court (ICC) have voted to dismiss Karim Khan as chief prosecutor for alleged sexual misconduct.Elected the ICC's
body: Members of the International Criminal Court (ICC) have voted to dismiss Karim Khan as chief prosecutor for alleged sexual misconduct.Elected the ICC's third prosecutor in 2021, Khan was suspended last month. The decision to remove him was passed with 82 votes in favour.The court's oversight body found in June he had committed a "serious breach of duty and serious misconduct" by engaging in an improper sexual relationship with a junior ICC staff member and seeking to stop her pursuing her complaint.Khan has repeatedly denied all the allegations against him. His lawyer said he would challenge "the lawfulness and fairness of the decision through all available legal mechanisms".It was not immediately clear what legal avenues remained open to the ousted prosecutor.In a statement after the vote, the ICC "took note" of the decision of the Special Session of the Assembly of States Parties - the 125 member states which voted to remove Khan. "The Court will continue to attach the utmost importance to maintaining a safe, inclusive, and respectful working environment for all personnel," the ICC statement said.The entire process, however, goes beyond the fate of a single prosecutor and could reshape the world's only permanent war‑crimes tribunal.The misconduct investigation has put the institution under a glaring spotlight, intensified divisions inside it and played out alongside an unprecedented campaign to weaken, and in fact dismantle, the ICC in its entirety.The fear among its supporters is that the court will emerge weakened and less able to face the gravest global threats.Khan, a prominent British lawyer, has been on voluntary leave to fight the allegations since May 2025. He remains suspended from practising law in the UK, after the Bar Standards Board imposed an interim ban while it conducts its own inquiry.He was unable to attend the vote, held in the United Nations headquarters in New York, because he is barred from entering the United States under sanctions imposed by the Trump administration over the ICC's investigation into alleged war crimes by Israeli officials in Gaza.Regardless of his removal, the controversy is unlikely to end there.The decision follows a highly sensitive process that has left the court under intense scrutiny.In May 2024, allegations that Khan had engaged in sexual misconduct involving a female staff member were reported to the ICC by a third party.The court's Independent Oversight Mechanism (IOM) opened an investigation, but the case was later closed after the alleged victim declined to participate.Critics of the process argued that the investigation had been mishandled, undermining confidence in the IOM.Investigators ultimately said there was insufficient evidence to substantiate the allegations.A second referral was made in October 2024. The matter was then transferred to the United Nations Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS), which conducted a broader investigation into allegations of sexual misconduct and abuse of authority.That inquiry ran from November 2024 to December 2025 and generated more than 5,000 pages of evidence and testimony.The OIOS findings were subsequently reviewed by a panel of three judges tasked with advising whether Khan's conduct amounted to serious misconduct, less serious misconduct, or no misconduct.The allegations have unfolded during a period of exceptional pressure on the ICC,  coinciding with wider political tensions.The United States imposed sanctions on Khan after he sought arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged crimes linked to the war in Gaza.Washington's attitude to the court in general has become increasingly hostile in recent years.Earlier this month, the US launched a new "whole‑of‑government" campaign to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick" in what it calls a threat to American sovereignty, promising visa bans, asset freezes and diplomatic pressure on allies to withdraw from the court or reject its jurisdiction over their nationals.The United States, Russia and Israel are not members of the ICC. However, the court can exercise jurisdiction over crimes committed by their nationals on the territory of ICC member states.

schema.headline: ICC top prosecutor removed over sexual misconduct allegations

title: Tintwistle Moor fire burning one month on is 'the size of a small town'
description: Image source, Derby Mountain Rescue TeamImage caption, Firefighters have been stationed on the Peak District moorland near Glossop for more than a mon
body: Image source, Derby Mountain Rescue TeamImage caption, Firefighters have been stationed on the Peak District moorland near Glossop for more than a month with no end in sightByIsaac AsheEast MidlandsAs darkness set in over the Peak District one Wednesday night in June, calls started to come in to Derbyshire's fire service over smoke starting to rise from the moorland overlooking the town.More than a month on, the Tintwistle Moor fire is now a sprawling, smouldering blaze the size of a small town, which can be seen from space.Declared a major incident on 13 July, it has come in tandem with a prolonged spell of hot, dry weather that shows little sign of easing soon, pushing the country's firefighting resources to their limits.Now Dr Kirsten Lees, environmental sciences lecturer, specialising in zero carbon at the University of Derby, has told the BBC Tintwistle is on a par with the biggest wildfires ever seen in England - and it's still burning.When questioned about her assertion the fire could be one of the largest in recent memory in England, she said: "It may well be, yes."Image source, Derbyshire Fire and Rescue ServiceImage caption, Dozens of firefighters are still fighting the fire more than one month on She added: "Honestly, it's upsetting and it's really scary."In the most recent years, we had Saddleworth in 2018. We had Fylingdales up in the North York Moors last year. And this is comparable in scale to both of those."My estimate is that it is about the size of a small town. As this is not out yet, we don't know how much bigger it's going to get."Analysis of data from the European Forest Fire Information System (Effis) by BBC Verify estimates the fire, which first began on 24 June, has burned 606 hectares (1,630 acres) - equivalent to 900 football pitches.This is larger than the footprint of Hadfield, one of the nearest towns to the wildfire and home to about 6,700 people.Lees - who has been monitoring the wildfire using satellite imagery - added: "In Wales we tend to have some large ones. In terms of being the largest fire that we've seen in the Peak District, it probably would need to grow another 25% or so to overtake the Saddleworth fire, and obviously Fylingdales was bigger again."Image caption, Analysis of data from the European Forest Fire Information System (Effis) by BBC Verify estimates total area burned by the fire at Tintwistle has reached 606 hectares A further wildfire at Dovestone Reservoir, north of the Tintwistle blaze, covers about 90 hectares (220 acres).Lees added: "At the moment the fire services have been doing a fantastic job keeping it under control as much as possible. We probably won't see this being completely out until we get some good rain."Clive Stanbrook, deputy chief fire officer for Derbyshire Fire and Rescue Service, said on Thursday the operation was "complex and challenging", which the brigade and partner agencies were working to bring to a "safe conclusion as quickly as possible".Firefighters said due to its vast scale, the ground affected had been divided into four sectors - Didsbury Sector, Crowden Sector, Arnfield Sector and Featherbed Moss Sector - to allow teams to focus resources on specific areas.Stanbrook said: "Around 65 firefighters from Derbyshire and across the UK, supported by partner organisations including the Fire Operations Group, are actively supporting the response to the Tintwistle Moor wildfire, with many more being rotated and mobilised when required."Thanks to their hard work, and the support of many colleagues behind the scenes, significant progress has been made."Figure caption, Watch: Drone footage - filmed last month - showed the initial scale of the moorland wildfireBut a huge issue for those on the ground - or in the skies, with helicopters providing support by dropping loads of water on to the wildfire - is what is actually burning.Lees said: "In the summer, we tend to get different types of vegetation igniting - woody shrubs, things like heather, and they burn much more intensely, which means that the fires can be not only large, but also severe as well."Once the wildfire gets into the peat, peat is a fuel, burned historically particularly in Scotland and Ireland, so it does burn incredibly well."Once the fire gets into that, it is incredibly vulnerable. We're struggling with ways to prevent the fire spreading once it gets into the peat and prevent it reigniting."Peak District National Park Authority ranger Kate Wilson, 40, from Buxton in the county, has been just one of those searching for hotspots in the peatland, and helping to keep the flames from spreading.Image source, Peak District National Park AuthorityImage caption, Ranger Kate Wilson is one of many searching for hotspotsShe said: "You've got your full firefighting kits, you've got all your tools, you're carrying water and you're trying to put out flaming moorland."It's really hot, really hard work, you get really dirty, but also you feel like you're doing good work and really helping the environment."You get competing emotions, you're frustrated that the fires happen, really sad to see the devastation, there should be heather and shrubs and grass and bilberries, you can walk past a nest of eggs that have been completely burnt out."But there's a real sense of camaraderie. We're a very small cog in a massive firefighting machine, everyone is working really hard in hard conditions."The fire can be devastating for wildlife. The flames destroy nests, kill fledglings, mammals, and insects unable to escape the fast-moving flames.Dr Kirsten Lees added: "It's really upsetting to see the impact that it's having on the vegetation, the plants and the wildlife."This is going to have a really, really devastating impact on the wildlife particularly our ground nesting birds so curlews, skylarks... things like that are really vulnerable to wildfires because they nest literally on the ground - they can't escape the flames so their chicks, their eggs, particularly late spring, early summer, they're really vulnerable."Image source, Peak District National Park AuthorityImage caption, Some animals simply cannot flee the flamesAnd once the fire is dampened down, the habitats needed to support fragile ecosystems are lost, sometimes for decades, Craig Best - National Trust general manager for the Peak District - said."These peatland habitats are vitally important for all of us," he said."They provide our drinking water, they store carbon, they're a great place for people to walk, and obviously they're essential for nature, but these fires can have a huge impact on these landscapes and it's particularly the peat soils we get concerned about."Every millimetre of peat takes approximately 100 years to accumulate."Figure caption, Watch: Footage shows ranger damping down "devastating" Tintwistle Moor fireWildfires come with a human impact too, above and beyond the obvious physical damage they cause to land and sometimes property.All smoke is potentially harmful to your health, according to advice from the UK Health Security Agency.Fine particles in the smoke, which can vary depending on what is being burned, can penetrate deep into your lungs and even enter your bloodstream causing illness.While short-term exposure is not usually an issue for healthy people, people with health conditions are more likely to be affected.Nicola Naylor, a farmer whose land sits near to Tintwistle, said: "The fire itself has been one of the most dramatic ones I've seen in the last 20 years, and the fire service's response is amazing."People are shocked at how much smoke there's been. People with health conditions, people that were older, children, were distressed by it."And Lees added: "When we do eventually get some rain, that run-off is going to go into our reservoirs and our water supply, and it's going to cost more to treat that to make sure it's clean for us."Image source, Peak District National Park AuthorityImage caption, Peat can smoulder and then reignite, making the challenge of putting the wildfire out even tougherRob Kenning, ranger team manager for the Peak District National Park Authority, said it was trialling using a seasonal ranger to patrol in the evenings to help prevent wildfires in the lighter, warmer summer months in areas likely to attract lots of tourists.He said council public spaces protection orders have also begun to be enforced, which can see people starting fires or using barbecues fined up to £1,000 in parts of the Peak District.He said: "Unfortunately, having many more visitors coming out to the park, we're pretty clear that this is going to be an ongoing problem and potentially an increasing problem."And it's not just the Peak District that is seeing a rise in wildfires.Image source, Derby Mountain Rescue TeamImage caption, The moorland and woodland on fire in Derbyshire is not the only major incident currently being tackled in the UKThe Fire Brigades Union (FBU) said more than 40,000 hectares burned last year in more than 1,000 incidents, while in 2026 fire and rescue services in England and Wales have responded to 342 wildfires up to 6 July, according to data from the National Fire Chiefs Council.The FBU is urging government to convene a National Wildfire Summit to build national resilience, and is calling for 5,000 firefighters to be recruited nationwide.Work is also being carried out to build resilience into the Peak District landscape itself.Lees said: "We've got ongoing projects looking at peatland restoration, raising the water levels, things like that."But peat stores a huge amount of carbon built up over hundreds, thousands of years and this gets burnt off in a matter of days, which then contributes to climate change which makes the wildfires worse and it becomes a vicious cycle."It used to be the case that I would talk about my work with wildfires in the UK and people would be surprised that we even had wildfires at all. And now it seems like we're seeing them every summer."Additional reporting by Matt Weigold, Alex Thorp, Steve Beech and Dan HuntGet in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Derby

schema.headline: Tintwistle Moor fire burning one month on is 'the size of a small town'

title: LeBron James to join Philadelphia 76ers after Los Angeles Lakers exit
description: LeBron James has announced he will be joining the Philadelphia 76ers next season for what he says will be his final contract in the NBA.The 41-year-ol
body: LeBron James has announced he will be joining the Philadelphia 76ers next season for what he says will be his final contract in the NBA.The 41-year-old, the highest points scorer in the history of the league, left the Los Angeles Lakers after eight years last month.  The Cleveland Cavaliers, Golden State Warriors, Minnesota Timberwolves and Miami Heat were also rumoured to be in the running for the four-time NBA champion."I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fanbase and start this incredible journey one last time," James said on X., externalJames has won an NBA title with all three teams he previously played for. He won two with Miami, who earlier this week mistakenly posted a link to an 'introductory press conference' for James.A Heat spokesperson told Reuters, external the video was posted in error by staff who were preparing for the possibility of James rejoining the team he played for between 2010 and 2014.Either side of that Miami stint, James had two spells with Cleveland, who drafted James in 2003 and are based near his hometown of Akron, Ohio."Miami I'll forever love and Northeast Ohio will always [be] home," James added.James helped the Cavs become NBA champions in 2016 and joined the Lakers in 2018, claiming another NBA title two years later.He has been named the NBA's Most Valuable Player four times, all between 2009 and 2013, and has been an NBA All-Star the last 22 seasons running.

schema.headline: LeBron James to join Philadelphia 76ers after Los Angeles Lakers exit

title: Teen who singer D4vd is accused of killing had multiple abortions, texts reveal
description: WARNING: Readers may find details in this article distressing.Texts between singer D4vd and Celeste Rivas Hernandez, the 14-year-old he is accused of
body: WARNING: Readers may find details in this article distressing.Texts between singer D4vd and Celeste Rivas Hernandez, the 14-year-old he is accused of murdering, reveal she had been pregnant and had had an abortion before her death. The messages were shown during a hearing for a judge to determine if the singer, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, should go on trial for the teen's death last year."What [if] the first abortion didn't work?" Celeste texted Burke in June 2024, according to prosecutors. She was 13 years old at the time and he was 19. Prosecutors say Burke killed her after she threatened to reveal he had been abusing a minor and destroy his career. He has pleaded not guilty to charges of murdering and sexually abusing the girl.In an exchange from January 2024, Burke apologised to the teen for "putting her through this", according to messages shown in the Los Angeles court on Friday.She responded, "neither of us are capable of watching and taking care of the baby. it's for the best no?"Burke asked, "also my mother always told me to ask this question if I was ever in this situation … it is mine right?" Celeste replied "of course its yours David", according to testimony from a detective.The court heard that in another text to Celeste, sent in June 2024, Burke wrote: "Let's let this abortion be the last one til we have the real one…" Prosecutors presented iCloud data recovered from the defendant's iPhone, showing texts between him and Celeste dating back to 8 August 2022, when she was 11 years old and Burke was 17.The phone belonging to Burke also had explicit photos of the teenager during the alleged sexual abuse, prosecutors and Los Angeles Police Detective Corey Farell said on Friday.The victim's mother, Mercedes Rivas Hernandez, became visibly emotional and left the court with her husband as details of some of the pictures were read aloud during the proceedings.D4vd, who rose to fame on TikTok with the viral hits Romantic Homicide and Here With Me, was on tour when police found Celeste's body in the front truck of his Tesla in September 2025 - the day after she would have turned 15. His worldwide tour was cancelled and he largely retreated from public life and social media.Police announced his arrest in April this year.Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman filed seven criminal charges against him, including murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child and the mutilation of remains.They said the teen was reported missing by her family and was last seen at Burke's Hollywood Hills home on 3 April 2025 - five months before her remains were discovered in the Tesla.Prosecutors have said he met Celeste online when she was 11, and allege he started sexually abusing her when she was 13 and he was 18.

title: Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJoe TidyCyber correspondent, BBC World ServiceThis week the tech world was gripped by a story that has it all - and which
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJoe TidyCyber correspondent, BBC World ServiceThis week the tech world was gripped by a story that has it all - and which started like a sci-fi thriller.Hugging Face - a kind of app store for artificial intelligence tools - announced on 16 July it had been hacked by a cyber criminal wielding enormously powerful AI.The bombshell announcement was full of scary, highly technical terms: "a swarm of sandboxes", "agentic attacker", and "self-migrating command and control".Hugging Face said the hack was different from anything it had handled before because it was done at superhuman speed by an AI with little or no human guidance.The AI performed 17,000 actions in less than two days, successfully breaching the large wealthy tech company to steal secrets.It left the tech world in shock. But who was responsible for this attack?Hugging Face researchers guessed the mysterious attackers had used one of the big AI models but they had no idea who or where the criminals were.The perplexed company contacted the police and investigations commenced.Who did it?Commentators and analysts took to their podcasts and social media accounts to guess which cyber crime group or nation state hacker might be behind it.Then on Wednesday, nearly a week after Hugging Face raised the alarm, the true culprit was unmasked.It was ChatGPT.The Scooby-Doo-style reveal was made even more bizarre - and worrying - because OpenAI said its bot did the whole thing on its own, without permission.The firm said it all went down during a test of its tech's hacking skills. Two new versions of ChatGPT, designed to be master hackers, broke out of a supposedly secure test environment and gained access to the internet.They then attacked Hugging Face to get access to the information to help them ace their exam.OpenAI issued a press release explaining what had happened and said it was "partnering with Hugging Face" to address the security incident and share lessons learned.Conspiracy dramaSince then, there has been fierce debate about the incident.Was it truly a stark warning about the future of AI? Or was it a publicity stunt by OpenAI to show off how powerful their models are?It's the kind of scare marketing AI companies have been accused of for years and, since the much discussed launch of Anthropic's Mythos model, cyber-security prowess has been a focal point.One of the top comments on OpenAI boss Sam Altman's X post about the incident summarises this scepticism: "If y'all can't understand that this was written to purely brag about the model then I don't know what to tell you."Figure caption, Watch: Why is the OpenAI cyber-attack so alarming?Cyber-security consultant Daniel Card said sarcastically on LinkedIn: "Isn't it lucky [that] out of the millions of sites that got pwn3d [hacked], OpenAI managed to pwn someone who also could benefit from the marketing exposure…"For some, the story is more conspiracy drama than sci-fi thriller. The message is: "Aren't my AI tools really powerful? Buy them so you can protect yourself from other people's AI attacks."We can't know the truth, but the opposing point of view posed by other commentators is just as dramatic. Is this a sign that OpenAI made a potentially dangerous error in judgement and planning?Comedy of errorsI've covered lots of AI stories, including the fears around Anthropic's Mythos model.My inbox is now chock full of cyber-security companies and experts criticising OpenAI for not building a stronger container to test its AI, known as a sandbox.After all, these AI agents had been trained specifically to hack into and out of places with no restrictions at all."The OpenAI and Hugging Face incident is a real-world example of a broader issue we've been highlighting for months," said Dor Sarig from Pillar Security. "Sandboxes alone are not a sufficient security boundary for agentic AI."Cyber security Professor Alan Woodward from Surrey University told reporters OpenAI had "egg on it's face", and Katie Moussouris from Luta Security went further, suggesting the AI industry is failing to control its dangerous inventions."We are working on cutting edge technology without the knowledge to contain it," she said. "Just because we have the smartest people developing AI does not mean we have the ability to do so safely."According to these views, if the hacking incident was a publicity stunt then it appears as though it backfired.Whatever led to the hack, it's clear this is a major moment for the AI industry and the cyber security world, which collided this year in ways people had been fearing for a long time.Addressing this fierce debate, AI and cyber security advisor Francesca Bosco said: "Two simplistic narratives are equally unhelpful: that this was a Hollywood-style escape, or that it was merely a publicity exercise. "A more serious interpretation is that a stress test exposed weaknesses in containment and evaluation architecture."Disaster movieThis event is the latest in a string of worrying and weird examples of AI agents going rogue.In recent research, the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) found frontier AI models are so fixated on completing tasks they "cheated" in tests to achieve their goals.The research from AISI came with this worrying warning: "A model that pursues a goal through unintended or unauthorised means may cause harm, particularly in high-stakes use cases."Inevitably, this OpenAI hack has further fuelled fears of what could happen if AI agents are let loose. Could they go rogue on a larger scale and cause some sort of disaster? This is particularly concerning with AI being used increasingly in warfare as seen in Iran and Ukraine.Ciaran Martin, former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, offered a calmer view. "It is a bit of a leap to go from this incident to saying that AI agents are going to take over drones and start killing people," he said.But for Martin, and many others, the story is undoubtedly another vivid example of something that 2026 is teaching us fast:AI agents are now very good hackers - and that is something we have to prepare for, urgently.

schema.headline: Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?

title: Ukraine's Zelensky struggles to fix crisis over removal of defence minister Fedorov
description: With an acting defence minister in place and a new commander-in-chief in charge of the military, Ukraine's recent political crisis is over, right?Not
body: With an acting defence minister in place and a new commander-in-chief in charge of the military, Ukraine's recent political crisis is over, right?Not so fast.The political fallout from President Volodymyr Zelensky's 15 July decision not to re-appoint Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister, as part of a cabinet reshuffle, continues to reverberate about Kyiv and beyond, even as air raid sirens wail and Russian drones and missiles are intercepted overhead.Fedorov's mostly young supporters are still mounting daily street protests, demanding that Zelensky reinstate the popular young innovator widely credited with driving much of Ukraine's recent technological innovation.On Thursday, Fedorov said he had rejected Zelensky's offers of alternative posts in government, saying there were only three positions worth having to influence the course of the war: minister of defence, commander-in-chief of the military or president of Ukraine."If you don't have a ministry under you, you don't have a budget," ex-deputy defence minister Alina Frolova said, "and you don't actually have the authority to do something."Fedorov's reference to the presidency did not go unnoticed. Was this the first public sign that the ousted minister sees himself as a rival to Zelensky?One former defence official suggested he became a real candidate for the presidency the moment he was dismissed.But with the country at war and no elections scheduled – Ukraine's constitution still prevents them in wartime – how useful is it to put your head above the political parapet so far in advance?"He's being childish," one opposition MP told me, on condition that he remained anonymous."He's looking to further his political career, which I think is just stupid in the circumstances where we are."The president's supporters say Zelensky has gone to great lengths to resolve the crisis, especially over the question of who to replace the unpopular commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi.Eventually he decided on Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43, a highly respected former commander of Ukraine's land forces."He consulted pretty much every significant figure in the Ukrainian army," former government adviser Yuriy Sak told the BBC earlier this week."So the decision that he has taken now is very well informed, and I support it because General Drapatyi is a young, battle-proven, modern general who will take our defences to a new level, hopefully."But while Drapatyi's appointment has been generally welcomed, it only represents a partial fix by a president scrambling to repair the damage caused by his removal of Fedorov.Ironically, for a president whose youth and apparent dynamism propelled him to power in 2019, Zelensky seems to have misjudged the mood of young Ukrainians, eager for their leaders – political and military – to represent their values and aspirations."It's quite natural that people want to see someone who is a warrior against corruption, who is very modern, who is young," Oleksandr Merezhko, an MP from Zelensky's Servant of the People party, said."People want to see something like that in politics, which they consider to be dirty and full of hypocrisy. They need heroes."But Merezhko agrees that Fedorov's ambitions and almost mythic, popular status may have brought about his downfall, especially for a president with a track record of sidelining those he sees as potential rivals."Don't outshine your master," Merezhko says, quoting from Robert Greene's 1998 self-help book, The 48 Laws of Power.Most analysts agree that last week's reshuffle had one overarching purpose: to cut Fedorov down to size. But Zelensky's strategy appears to have backfired."His removal has led to the opposite result," Merezhko says. "His rating soared. Just soared."Few doubt Fedorov's commitment, imagination and drive, but some question whether his outsized reputation is fully justified.They point out that he inherited a situation in which Ukraine had already successfully built up its medium- and long-range strike capabilities, something over which the defence minister has little day-to-day influence."The energy and clarity he brought to the job was impressive and he showed immense personal courage," a former European defence official said. "But the thing that will carry on regardless is the innovation culture. It's 2,000 companies, not a single individual."One opposition MP, who asked not to be identified, put it more bluntly."Ninety-nine per cent of these young people on the street have no clue how the ministry of defence is operating, how the general staff is operating," he said."They think Fedorov is good because he wants to fight with drones and Syrskyi was bad because he was looking for people to fight. It's a dramatic simplification which is totally wrong."But understandable, perhaps, in a country exhausted by 12 years of war with Russia. Who would not want to believe that drones and robots can do the job, rather than a member of your own family, roughly conscripted on the streets of your own hometown?Everyone agrees that Ukraine needs to put this politically toxic episode behind it before summer gives way to autumn and the country braces itself for another Russian assault on its energy grid."We need to prepare for how we will get through the winter," Zelensky said on the Telegram messaging app on Thursday.Politicians and experts interviewed for this piece mostly agree that while the political damage of this episode continues to undermine President Zelensky's authority and reputation, Ukraine is unlikely to experience significant setbacks on the battlefield.What Zelensky calls his "long-range sanctions" campaign against Russia is in full swing, causing mounting damage to the Russian economy. Ukraine's long front lines, meanwhile, remain largely static, thanks to a 15-30km (9-18-mile) wide "kill zone" where anything or anyone who moves is observed and attacked by drones.As a young, still relatively immature democracy, Ukraine's institutions have been put under colossal strain by Russia's full-scale invasion. But, many argue, the country remains resilient and resourceful."The secret of Ukraine's success is that we are much stronger horizontally than vertically," opposition MP Andrii Osadchuk told me."I hope the damage will be minimal."

schema.headline: Ukraine's Zelensky struggles to fix crisis over removal of defence minister Fedorov

title: Jurgen Klopp: Germany boss threatens to quit new job if media invade family's privacy

body: Jurgen Klopp started his reign as Germany's head coach by threatening to quit if the media invades his family's privacy.The former Liverpool manager was appointed on a four-year deal on Friday to replace Julian Nagelsmann, who resigned this month after Germany's shock World Cup defeat by Paraguay in the last 32.But the 59-year-old issued a warning to the media as he held his first news conference as Germany's head coach."If you behave badly and don't leave my family in peace then I'll be gone, I'll just turn away," Klopp said."I know there are other countries where national team coaches are treated even worse."I'm not doing this job for myself, I'm doing it for you. I'm taking this job even though I've seen how you've treated Julian Nagelsmann and Thomas Tuchel."I love this job but I am always ready to call it quits if need be."Both Nagelsmann and England boss Tuchel came under media scrutiny after their exits from the World Cup, with Tuchel criticised for his defensive tactics and substitutions as the Three Lions let slip a 1-0 lead in their semi-final defeat by Argentina.Klopp's appointment was widely expected for weeks and his contract will see him through to the 2030 World Cup, co-hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco."Jurgen Klopp is not going to have any 'career' after the national team," he added. "This is the pinnacle, the absolutely high point of my footballing career as coach. I will give everything I have got."

schema.headline: Jurgen Klopp: Germany boss threatens to quit new job if media invade family's privacy
